TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Abir means crossing from one side of a river or road to the other. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The verb ʿabara describes crossing a road or river from one side to the other. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The author answers the comparison with minor impurity by saying it occurs often and cleansing it would cause hardship; the verse's crossing exception suffices. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): ʿĀbir means crossing or passing through; the cited verse uses عبر for traversing the heat of midday. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī understands the passer as someone who walks through a mosque without staying there. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزمخشري): On the reading of prayer as the mosque, al-Zamakhsharī takes the exception to permit only passing through on a route to water, where water is in the mosque, or after a wet dream there. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (علي وابن عباس وابن جبير ومجاهد والحكم): These authorities identify the passer as a traveler: a junub may not approach prayer until washing, except a traveler may use tayammum. Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, Mālik, al-Thawrī, and others bar even mosque passage. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): One parse makes عابري a circumstantial exception governed by the prohibition: do not approach in janāba except while traveling or crossing a mosque, depending on the interpretation. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari takes the exception as a circumstantial phrase from the addressees generally, with travel as an additional excuse and crossing the path as its expression. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (غير مسمى): One interpretation supplies an omitted مضاف: ‘the places of prayer,’ meaning mosques; the exception for crossing a path supports this in one reading. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas interprets the exception as allowing a junub person to pass through a mosque without sitting; Ibn Kathir lists many authorities who agree, including Ibn Masud, Anas, Abu Ubayda, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, Qatada, and others. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن جرير): Ibn Jarir explains an abir al-sabil as one who passes and crosses through; Arabic uses the same root for crossing a road or river and calls a camel able to cross journeys abir asfar. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud interprets the exception as passing through the mosque; he elsewhere permits a junub person to cross it in transit. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الشافعي): On the mosque interpretation of prayer, crossing through a mosque is allowed for a junub person; al-Shafi'i holds this, while the well-known Hanafi position forbids mosque entry absolutely. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (من حمل الصلاة على مواضعها): One parsing takes prayer as its locations and crossing as passing through them, so the later condition states a distinct rule. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The recommended pause after “until you wash” and the spatial language of approaching, crossing, and travel support that interpretation. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الكثير): Many commentators take the passage otherwise than the spatial interpretation of prayer and crossing. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): In Arabic, a traveler while on a journey is an “ʿābir al-sabīl,” from crossing or passing through a river or road. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Al-ṣalāt here means the mosque, because the exception for passers-through fits a rule about a junub entering the mosque. STUDYQURAN (author): The exception covers junub travelers seeking temporary shelter in a mosque and Companions whose adjacent homes required crossing the Prophet’s mosque to leave.
